1a.html:
Economic development is a sustained rise in the well-being of a nation's people, brought about by growth in output together with structural and institutional change.

  • Traditional view: sustained growth of GNI and income per capita faster than population, with the share of agriculture falling and that of industry and services rising.
  • New economic view: development must improve well-being more broadly. Seers asked what has happened to poverty, unemployment and inequality; if they have grown worse, it is not development even if per capita income doubled.
  • Sen's capabilities approach: what matters is what people can be and do (live long, be healthy, literate, take part in community life). Development expands these freedoms.
  • Its three objectives are more life-sustaining goods, higher levels of living and a wider range of economic and social choices. The course deck sums it up as economic progress with social well-being and environmental protection.

Developing economically but still underdeveloped ("growth without development")

  1. Resource enclave: Equatorial Guinea's oil gives a GNI per capita of about USD 19,500 (PPP), yet its HDI is 0.591 and life expectancy 57.9 years, below Bangladesh (USD 3,677, HDI 0.608). Elites capture the oil rents.
  2. Pakistan against Bangladesh: Pakistan has the higher income per capita (USD 5,311) but the lower HDI (0.562), with lower female literacy, higher child mortality and higher fertility.
  3. Hypothetical, unequal growth: GDP grows 7% a year, but gains go to a few owners while unemployment and poverty rise.
  4. Hypothetical, unsustainable growth: output rises by clearing forests and polluting rivers, cutting future living standards.

Growth is therefore necessary but not sufficient for development.
pts: Traditional meaning: sustained growth of GNI and income per capita above population growth, with structural change
Broader meaning: improvement in well-being, with falling poverty, unemployment and inequality (Seers)
Sen's capabilities: development as expanding what people can be and do (functionings, freedom)
States the three objectives of development, or economic progress with social well-being and environmental protection

A first example (real or hypothetical) of high income or growth with poor social outcomes, with the reason, for example Equatorial Guinea: about USD 19,500 (PPP) but HDI 0.591, oil rents captured by elites
A second example, for example Pakistan's higher income but lower HDI than Bangladesh, or Gabon or the Gulf oil states
Examples of another kind: growth with rising inequality, unemployment or poverty, or growth that destroys the environment (real or hypothetical)
Concludes that growth is necessary but not sufficient
1a.src: Ch 1 Economic development (Todaro), slides 16-23; Dimensions of economic development (v3), slides 8-13; Ch 2 Comparative development, slides 22-23; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 10-13, 25-27
1a.watch:
• "Economic development" is not "economic growth": growth is a rise in output, development a rise in well-being. Say so explicitly.
  • The example must show growth or high income together with poor social outcomes; a poor country with low growth is not an example.
  • The HDI table on the slide is from the 2018 Human Development Report; quote the figures as approximate and give the year if you can.

1b.html:
Definitions. The GDP growth rate is the annual percentage increase in real GDP. The poverty rate is the share of people below the national upper poverty line (cost of basic needs), measured by the Household Income and Expenditure Survey (HIES); the lower line gives extreme poverty.

Trend of GDP growth (2008 to 2022, from the chart). Growth stayed between about 5 and 8% every year except one: about 6.0% in 2008, 5.0% in the 2009 world recession, 6 to 7% through the 2010s, a peak of 7.9% in 2019, 3.4% in the 2020 pandemic, and a rebound to 7.1% in 2022, an average of about 6.3%. The fitted trend rises by about 0.08 points a year, while Pakistan's falls. Real GDP roughly doubled (about 2.1 times) from 2010 to 2022, and GDP per capita rose from about USD 780 to about USD 2,690.

Trend of poverty (HIES). Poverty fell from 31.5% (2010) to 24.3% (2016) and 18.7% (2022), 12.8 points or about 1.1 points a year; extreme poverty fell from 17.6% to 12.9% and 5.6%.

Explanation and justification. Fast, steady growth has been pro-poor, so it counts as development, not just growth:

  1. Labour-intensive garment exports gave jobs to millions of low-skilled workers, mostly women.
  2. Remittances flowed directly to rural households.
  3. Higher farm productivity and rural roads and electricity raised rural incomes.
  4. Safety nets, microfinance and NGO programmes reached the poor.
  5. Social indicators moved with income: life expectancy rose from 69.6 (2010) to 73.3 years (2022) and infant mortality fell from about 39 to about 23 per 1,000.

Qualifications. Poverty fell more slowly in 2016-22 (0.93 points a year) than in 2010-16 (1.2); inequality has widened; growth slowed to 5.82% in FY 2023-24 (provisional) while inflation rose; and some observers question the official growth figures. Growth alone is necessary but not sufficient.

Conclusion: the trends justify calling Bangladesh's growth development, since high growth went with a large fall in poverty, but sustaining it now needs broader, more equal growth.
pts: Defines the GDP growth rate (real GDP change) and the poverty rate (headcount below the national line, HIES)
Growth trend with values: about 5 to 8% a year, peak 7.9% (2019), 3.4% dip (2020), rebound to about 7%; average about 6.3%
Growth is steady and trending up (slope about +0.08 points a year, against Pakistan's falling trend), or per capita income rising (about USD 780 to 2,690)
Poverty trend: 31.5% to 24.3% to 18.7% (2010-2022) and extreme poverty 17.6% to 12.9% to 5.6%
Quantifies the fall: about 12.8 points, or about 1.1 points a year
Explains why growth reduced poverty: labour-intensive RMG jobs, remittances, agriculture and rural infrastructure, safety nets
Justifies development beyond growth with social indicators (life expectancy, infant mortality)
Qualifications: slower poverty decline, rising inequality, recent slowdown and inflation, or data doubts
Reasoned conclusion
1b.watch:
• Growth values are read off the slide chart (World Bank series, about plus or minus 0.2 points). For Bangladesh that series is the official fiscal-year one, filed under the year the fiscal year ends: 2019 is FY 2018-19 (7.88%) and 2020 is FY 2019-20 (3.45%). Quoting either the year or the fiscal year is accepted.
  • Slide 65's 2000 lower-line rural and urban values (39.5% and 13.7%, below 2005's 14.6%) appear to be the 1995-96 figures; the HIES 2000 values are about 38% and 20%. Use the national columns, which are correct.
  • HIES surveys are only every five or six years, so the poverty "trend" has three points in 15 years; do not invent annual poverty rates.
  • The poverty-in-Bangladesh chart (slide 69) shows a spike to about 42% in 2020; that is a pandemic survey estimate from a different method, not HIES, and should not be joined to the HIES series.

2a.fix: • hum-ch2 slides 14 and 20 say the education index uses a geometric mean and the maxima are the observed maxima. That was the 2010 to 2013 method. Since the 2014 Report the goalposts are fixed (85 yr, 18 yr, 15 yr, USD 75,000) and the education index is the arithmetic mean of the two schooling indices (hum-hdr p 2).
2a.html:
How the NHDI is calculated

The New HDI (NHDI), used by UNDP since 2010, is a composite index from 0 to 1 of average achievement in health, knowledge and living standard.

  1. Dimension indices. Each indicator is scaled between fixed goalposts: I = (\text{actual} - \text{min})/(\text{max} - \text{min}).
    • Health: life expectancy at birth, 20 to 85 yr.
    • Education: expected years of schooling (0 to 18) and mean years of schooling (0 to 15), averaged.
    • Income: GNI per capita at 2011 purchasing power parity (PPP: rates that equalise the cost of a common basket), USD 100 to 75,000, in natural logs because of diminishing marginal utility.
  2. Geometric mean: \mathrm{HDI} = (I_H \times I_E \times I_I)^{1/3}. A weak dimension is not fully offset by a strong one (imperfect substitutability).

Example, Bangladesh (HDR 2019): I_H = 0.805, I_E = 0.514, I_I = 0.559, so \mathrm{HDI} = (0.805 \times 0.514 \times 0.559)^{1/3} = 0.614, medium human development (0.550 to 0.699).

What I would do differently, and why

  • Adjust for inequality. Report an inequality-adjusted HDI as the headline, because national averages hide gaps by income, gender and region.
  • Measure quality as well as quantity. Use learning-adjusted schooling (test scores) and healthy life expectancy, because a year of school in Mali teaches less than one in Norway, and a bedridden year is not a year of full capability.
  • Prefer achievements to forecasts. Replace expected years of schooling, a UN projection that can be optimistic in poor countries, with completion rates.
  • Add missing freedoms. Include political and civil freedom or environmental sustainability, because development is the expansion of freedoms, and an HDI built on depleting resources cannot last.
  • Test the weights. Equal weights and the goalposts are value judgements; publish rankings under alternative weights to show how robust they are.
pts: Defines the NHDI: a composite 0 to 1 index of health, knowledge and living standard
Four indicators with goalposts: life expectancy 20 to 85 yr, expected schooling 0 to 18, mean schooling 0 to 15, GNI per capita USD 100 to 75,000 PPP (the slides' observed maxima also accepted)
Dimension index = (actual - min)/(max - min); education index as the mean of the two schooling indices (arithmetic, or the slides' geometric version)
Income index in natural logs because of diminishing marginal utility of income
\mathrm{HDI} = (I_H I_E I_I)^{1/3}, the geometric mean, with imperfect substitutability between dimensions
Works an example to a value and class, for example Bangladesh 0.614 (medium) or the slides' Ghana 0.558
A first change with its reason, for example an inequality adjustment because averages hide the distribution
A second change with its reason, for example quality-adjusted schooling or health because years are not learning or healthy life
A third change with its reason, for example forecasts replaced by achievements, added freedoms or environment, or tested weights (any sound change with a reason earns the credit)
2a.src: Ch 2 Comparative development, slides 13-20; HDR 2019 technical notes, pp 2-3; Dimensions of economic development (v3), slides 15-19; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 92-94, 145
2a.watch:
• The second part is open: marks go to the reason, not to a particular change. A change with no reason earns little.
  • UNDP already publishes some of these: the inequality-adjusted HDI (IHDI), the Gender Inequality Index and, since 2020, a planetary-pressures-adjusted HDI. Naming them shows the idea is workable.
  • Any redesign must stay computable for about 190 countries; Todaro notes that the HDI indicators were chosen partly because data exist.
  • The Ghana example (hum-ch2 slide 19) uses the 2010 to 2013 version (observed maxima, geometric-mean education index); either version earns credit if the goalposts are stated.

2b.html:
Definitions. GDP per capita is GDP divided by population (here in current US dollars), a measure of average income. The inflation rate is the annual percentage rise in the consumer price index. I compare Bangladesh with Sri Lanka and Pakistan.

GDP per capita

  • Bangladesh rose steadily (flat in 2000-02, then up every year) from about USD 410 (2000) to about USD 780 (2010) and USD 2,690 (2022): about 6.5 times. The step in 2016 partly reflects a rebasing of national accounts.
  • Sri Lanka has been richer throughout: about USD 870 (2000), a peak of about USD 4,390 (2017), then a fall to about USD 3,350 (2022) in its debt and foreign-exchange crisis. The gap shrank from about 2.1 times Bangladesh's level to about 1.25 times.
  • Pakistan was ahead of Bangladesh in the 2000s but grew slowly and unevenly; Bangladesh overtook it in the second half of the 2010s, and Pakistan's GDP per capita was roughly USD 1,500 to 1,700 in 2022.

Inflation (2001 to 2023)

  • Bangladesh was moderate and stable: 2 to 11.4% (peak 2011), about 5.5 to 5.7% in 2016-21, averaging about 6.6%, then rising to 7.7% (2022) and 7.9% (2023).
  • Pakistan was higher and far more volatile: from 2.5% (2015) to spikes of 20.3% (2008) and 23.6% (2023), averaging about 9.3%; its swings are about three times Bangladesh's.
  • Sri Lanka had moderate inflation in the 2010s but an extreme spike in 2022 (an annual average of roughly 45 to 50%) after its reserves ran out and the rupee collapsed.

Reasons. Bangladesh's steady growth came from garment exports, remittances and cautious macroeconomic management (moderate deficits and debt, a managed exchange rate). Sri Lanka's fall came from heavy foreign borrowing, tax cuts, a ban on chemical fertiliser and lost tourism, ending in default in 2022. Pakistan's lag came from political instability, energy shortages, repeated balance-of-payments crises and IMF programmes, with sharp currency falls feeding inflation.

Conclusion: Bangladesh has had the fastest and steadiest income growth of the three and the most stable prices, though its inflation has risen since 2022.
pts: Defines GDP per capita and the inflation rate (CPI change)
Chooses two South Asian countries and compares both variables for each (Sri Lanka and Pakistan here; India or another country with correct data also earns this)
Bangladesh GDP per capita trend: about USD 410 to 2,690 (2000-2022), steady, about 6.5-fold
Comparison with the first country, for example Sri Lanka higher but falling after 2017, gap narrowing from about 2.1 to 1.25 times
Comparison with the second country, for example Bangladesh overtaking Pakistan in the 2010s
Bangladesh inflation trend: moderate (about 5 to 8%, peak 11.4% in 2011, about 6.6% average), rising after 2021
Comparison of inflation with the first country, for example Pakistan higher and volatile (20.3% in 2008, 23.6% in 2023)
Comparison of inflation with the second country, for example Sri Lanka's 2022 spike
Reasons for the differences (RMG and remittances; Sri Lanka's debt crisis; Pakistan's instability and currency falls)
Reasoned conclusion
2b.watch:
• The slides give only Sri Lanka for GDP per capita (slide 36) and Pakistan for inflation (slide 62); the Pakistan per capita and Sri Lanka inflation values here are standard World Bank-type figures from memory, so they are given as approximate ranges. Quote years with every number.
  • Values are read off the slide charts (about plus or minus USD 50 and 0.3 points); the Bangladesh inflation values are the slide's data labels.
  • Use current-dollar GDP per capita for comparison only with care: exchange-rate swings (Sri Lanka 2022, Pakistan 2023) move it sharply even when real output changes little.

3a.html:
Project evaluation is the systematic assessment of whether a project is worth the resources it uses, done before, during and after it is carried out.

Stages of project evaluation (the project cycle)

  1. Identification: ideas are screened against national plan priorities and needs (pre-feasibility).
  2. Preparation (feasibility study): technical, market, financial and environmental study of alternative sites, scales and technologies; costs and benefits estimated year by year.
  3. Appraisal (ex-ante evaluation): an independent check in steps. Financial analysis at market prices tests profitability to the owner; economic analysis at shadow prices removes taxes and subsidies (transfers) and adds externalities; social analysis weights benefits to poor groups and regions. The criteria below decide. (In Bangladesh the Planning Commission usually appraises the project proposal, the DPP, and ECNEC approves the larger ones.)
  4. Implementation and monitoring (mid-term evaluation): cost, time and targets are tracked so problems are corrected.
  5. Ex-post evaluation: actual costs and benefits are compared with the forecasts; lessons feed back into new projects.

Four benefit-cost criteria (r = discount rate)

CriterionMeasureAccept if
NPV\sum (B_t - C_t)/(1+r)^t\mathrm{NPV} > 0
BCRPV(B)/PV(C)\mathrm{BCR} > 1
IRRrate at which NPV = 0\mathrm{IRR} > r
Paybackyears to recover the investmentwithin the cut-off

The best criterion is NPV. It uses all flows over the whole life, allows for the time value of money, measures the value added in taka and is additive, so it ranks mutually exclusive projects correctly. The others have flaws: payback ignores flows after recovery; IRR ignores scale, may have several values and assumes reinvestment at the IRR; BCR also ignores scale. At 10%, project S (Tk 10,000 returning Tk 15,000 after a year) has IRR 50% but NPV Tk 3,636; L (Tk 100,000 returning Tk 130,000) has IRR 30% but NPV Tk 18,182: choose L. BCR helps rank under a budget limit.
pts: Defines project evaluation as the systematic assessment of a project's worth before, during and after implementation
Early stages: identification against plan priorities, and preparation or feasibility study of alternatives
Appraisal in steps: financial analysis at market prices, economic analysis at shadow prices (transfers out, externalities in), social or distributional analysis
Later stages: implementation with monitoring or mid-term evaluation, and ex-post evaluation feeding lessons back
Four criteria, each with its measure and rule: NPV > 0, BCR > 1, IRR > discount rate, payback within the cut-off (1 each)
Names NPV as the best, with reasons: all flows, time value, value in taka, additive, correct ranking
Gives the weaknesses of the others (payback ignores later flows; IRR scale, multiple values or reinvestment; BCR scale)
Supports the choice with an example such as projects S and L, or notes the role of BCR under a budget limit
3a.src: Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 607-610; CBA exam note, pp 5-9, 12; Solved problems: NPV, IRR, payback, p 4; Cost-benefit analysis handout, handout parts VIII and XII; Standard textbook treatment
3a.watch:
• The slides do not list "stages of project evaluation". The project cycle above is the usual reading; a student who explains the appraisal stages instead (Todaro's objectives, shadow prices and social discount rate, decision criterion, or the UNIDO financial, economic, savings, distribution and merit-good stages) should earn the stage marks.
  • "Four benefit-cost criteria" are the course's NPV, IRR, BCR and payback; discounted payback or the profitability index may replace payback.
  • The Bangladesh route (DPP prepared by the ministry, Planning Commission appraisal, ECNEC approval above a cost threshold, IMED monitoring) is outside the slides; the approval threshold has changed over time, so do not quote one.
  • Do not call IRR the best because it is a percentage: when NPV and IRR conflict for mutually exclusive projects, follow NPV.

3b.html:
Definitions (end-of-year flows, year 0 = now, discount rate r):

  • NPV is the present value of benefits minus the present value of costs, \mathrm{NPV} = \sum_{t=0}^{n} (B_t - C_t)/(1+r)^t. Accept if positive: the project returns more than the opportunity cost of its resources. NPV = 0 means it earns exactly r.
  • BCR is benefit per taka of cost, \mathrm{BCR} = PV(B)/PV(C). Accept if above 1, which is the same test as \mathrm{NPV} > 0.
  • IRR is the discount rate that makes NPV zero, \sum (B_t - C_t)/(1+\mathrm{IRR})^t = 0, found by trial and interpolation. Accept if it exceeds the social discount rate.

Example: Tk 100,000 now and Tk 40,000, 50,000, 60,000 in years 1 to 3 at 10% give PV(B) = Tk 122,765, NPV = Tk 22,765, BCR = 1.23 and IRR = 21.6%.

Interpretation. Given: NPV = Tk 1,092,651.30 lakh, BCR = 1.893, IRR = 23.38%.

  • NPV is positive. Discounted benefits exceed discounted costs by Tk 1,092,651.30 lakh (Tk 10,926.5 crore, about Tk 109 billion) at the chosen discount rate. The project adds this net value to society, so it should be accepted.
  • BCR is 1.893. Each Tk 1 of present-value cost returns Tk 1.89 of present-value benefit. The margin is wide: benefits could fall 47% (1 - 1/1.893), or costs rise 89%, before BCR reaches 1.
  • IRR is 23.38%. The resources earn 23.38% a year, well above the social discount rates commonly used (roughly 8 to 12%). NPV stays positive at any rate below 23.38%, so the decision is robust to the choice of rate.
  • Implied size. From \mathrm{NPV} = B - C and \mathrm{BCR} = B/C:
C = \frac{\mathrm{NPV}}{\mathrm{BCR} - 1} = \frac{1{,}092{,}651.30}{0.893} = 1{,}223{,}574\ \text{lakh Tk}, \qquad B = 1.893\,C = 2{,}316{,}225\ \text{lakh Tk}

Answer: all three criteria agree: the project is economically viable and should be approved, subject to sensitivity analysis.
pts: NPV defined as PV(B) - PV(C) with the formula \sum (B_t - C_t)/(1+r)^t
NPV rule: accept if positive; NPV = 0 means the project earns exactly the discount rate
BCR defined as PV(B)/PV(C), accept if above 1
IRR defined as the discount rate giving NPV = 0, accept if above the social discount rate (found by trial and interpolation)
Interprets the NPV: discounted benefits exceed discounted costs by Tk 1,092,651.30 lakh (about Tk 10,927 crore); accept
Interprets the BCR: Tk 1.89 of benefit per Tk 1 of cost, above 1
Interprets the IRR: 23.38% exceeds the social discount rate (none is given; roughly 8 to 12% is common); NPV positive at any rate below it
Robustness: benefits may fall about 47% or costs rise about 89% before BCR = 1, or the implied PV of costs (about Tk 1,223,574 lakh) and benefits (about Tk 2,316,225 lakh)
Concludes that all three agree and the project should be approved
3b.src: CBA exam note, pp 5-9; Solved problems: NPV, IRR, payback, pp 1-2; Cost-benefit analysis handout, handout parts IV, V, VII and X; Standard textbook treatment
3b.watch:
• The unit is lakh taka: Tk 1,092,651.30 lakh is Tk 10,926.5 crore, not Tk 1.09 million.
  • The implied PVs assume BCR is the gross ratio PV(B)/PV(C) at the same rate as the NPV; a net BCR gives different figures.
  • The question gives no discount rate. The 8 to 12% range is indicative of rates development agencies have used, not a slide figure; any stated, reasonable rate earns the IRR mark.
  • A high BCR with a moderate IRR is not a contradiction: compare HUM 2020-21 (BCR 1.275, IRR 45.37%). IRR rises when benefits come early; BCR is high when benefits are large relative to costs.

4a.html:
The fundamental equation (equation of motion) of the Solow model gives the change in capital per worker over time.

Step 1. Production function per worker. Y = F(K, L) has constant returns to scale: zY = F(zK, zL) for any z > 0. Putting z = 1/L:

\frac{Y}{L} = F\!\left(\frac{K}{L}, 1\right) \;\Rightarrow\; y = f(k), \qquad y = \frac{Y}{L},\; k = \frac{K}{L}

Step 2. Saving equals investment. With no government, y = c + i. The consumption function is c = (1 - s)y, where s is the saving rate, so

i = y - c = s\,y = s f(k)

Step 3. Capital accumulation. Investment adds to the capital stock and depreciation at rate \delta removes from it:

\Delta K = I - \delta K = sY - \delta K

Step 4. Population growth. The labour force grows at the exogenous rate n: \Delta L / L = n.

Step 5. Change in k. The growth rate of a ratio is the growth rate of the numerator minus that of the denominator:

\frac{\Delta k}{k} = \frac{\Delta K}{K} - \frac{\Delta L}{L} = \frac{sY - \delta K}{K} - n

Multiplying by k = K/L:

\Delta k = \frac{sY}{L} - \delta\frac{K}{L} - nk \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\Delta k = s f(k) - (\delta + n)\,k}

Interpretation. s f(k) is actual investment per worker; (\delta + n)k is break-even investment: \delta k replaces worn-out capital and nk equips the new workers. Otherwise the capital stock is spread more thinly over a larger workforce.

Step 6. Steady state. \Delta k = 0 when

s f(k^*) = (\delta + n)\,k^*

Below k^* investment exceeds break-even and k rises; above it, k falls. So k^* is stable.

Result. Faster population growth raises break-even investment and lowers k^* and y^*. In the steady state k and y are constant, while total output Y grows at rate n.
pts: Uses constant returns (z = 1/L) to write y = f(k) with y = Y/L, k = K/L
From y = c + i and c = (1-s)y: investment i = s y = s f(k) (saving equals investment)
Capital accumulation \Delta K = I - \delta K
Labour force grows at rate n: \Delta L/L = n
Growth rate of k = growth rate of K minus n, then multiplies by k
Final equation \Delta k = s f(k) - (\delta + n)k
Explains break-even investment: \delta k for depreciation and nk to equip new workers
Steady state s f(k^*) = (\delta + n)k^*, stable from both sides (in words or on a diagram)
4a.src: Solow model (Mankiw ch 8), slides 8-17, 40-44; Mankiw, Macroeconomics, ch 8
4a.watch:
• The growth-rate step is exact in continuous time (\dot k = s f(k) - (\delta + n)k). In discrete periods the exact form is \Delta k = [s f(k) - (\delta + n)k]/(1 + n), which the slide form approximates for small n.
  • Do not write \Delta k = s f(k) - \delta k here: that is the model without population growth, the other paper's question.
  • From the steady state the golden rule follows: c^* = f(k^*) - (\delta + n)k^* is largest where \mathrm{MPK} = \delta + n (slide 46). It is not asked here.

4b.html:
Given: Y = K^{1/4} L^{3/4}; saving rate s = 0.3; depreciation rate \delta = 0.06; no population growth is given, so n = 0.

Find: the per-worker production function and the steady-state capital per worker k^*.

Step 1. Constant returns. The exponents add to 1/4 + 3/4 = 1, so the function has constant returns to scale and can be written per worker.

Step 2. Per-worker form. Divide both sides by L:

\frac{Y}{L} = \frac{K^{1/4} L^{3/4}}{L} = K^{1/4} L^{-1/4} = \left(\frac{K}{L}\right)^{1/4}

With y = Y/L and k = K/L:

\boxed{y = f(k) = k^{1/4}}

Output per worker depends only on capital per worker, with diminishing returns (the exponent is below 1).

Step 3. Equation of motion. Investment per worker is i = s y = s f(k), so

\Delta k = s f(k) - \delta k

Step 4. Steady state. Capital per worker is constant when \Delta k = 0, that is, investment just covers depreciation:

\begin{aligned} s\,(k^*)^{1/4} &= \delta\,k^* \\ (k^*)^{3/4} &= \frac{s}{\delta} = \frac{0.3}{0.06} = 5 \\ k^* &= 5^{4/3} = 8.55 \end{aligned}

In general, k^* = (s/\delta)^{1/(1-\alpha)} for y = k^{\alpha}.

The other per-worker values follow: y^* = 5^{1/3} = 1.71, i^* = 0.3 \times 1.71 = 0.513 = \delta k^*, c^* = 0.7 \times 1.71 = 1.20.

Answer: y = k^{1/4}; steady-state capital per worker k^* = 5^{4/3} \approx 8.55 units.
pts: Notes constant returns: exponents 1/4 + 3/4 = 1, so the per-worker form exists
Divides by L: Y/L = K^{1/4}L^{3/4}/L = (K/L)^{1/4}
Per-worker production function y = k^{1/4}
Equation of motion \Delta k = s f(k) - \delta k, with i = s f(k)
Steady-state condition \Delta k = 0, so s f(k^*) = \delta k^*
Substitutes: 0.3 (k^*)^{1/4} = 0.06 k^*, so (k^*)^{3/4} = 5
Inverts the exponent correctly: k^* = (s/\delta)^{4/3} (or the general (s/\delta)^{1/(1-\alpha)})
k^* = 5^{4/3} \approx 8.55 (8.5 to 8.6 accepted)
4b.src: Solow model (Mankiw ch 8), slides 8, 15-17, 26-30; Mankiw, Macroeconomics, ch 8
4b.watch:
• (k^*)^{3/4} = 5 gives k^* = 5^{4/3}, not 5^{3/4} = 3.34; invert the exponent.
  • Without population growth, break-even investment is \delta k. A student who adds a symbol n and sets n = 0 gets the same result.
  • The question defines c and i, so writing y^*, i^* and c^* is good practice, but only k^* is asked.

5a.html:
Industrialisation is the structural shift of output, exports and jobs from agriculture to manufacturing. In Bangladesh industry is over a third of GDP, led by ready-made garments (RMG, about 84% of exports).

Prospects

  1. Demographic dividend: a young labour force of 7.35 crore (2023) with low wages suits labour-intensive manufacturing.
  2. Proven export base: Bangladesh is one of the two largest garment exporters, with many certified green factories; RMG creates backward linkages (spinning, dyeing, accessories, packaging).
  3. Emerging sectors: pharmaceuticals (most domestic demand met, exports to many countries), leather and footwear, light engineering, shipbuilding, electronics, ICT and agro-processing.
  4. Infrastructure and zones: the Padma Bridge, Karnaphuli tunnel, Matarbari deep-sea port, expanded power capacity and the planned 100 economic zones.
  5. Home and regional markets: over 170 million consumers with remittance-fed demand, between the Indian and Chinese markets.

Challenges

  1. Narrow base: dependence on one product and a few markets makes the economy fragile.
  2. Energy and land: gas and power shortages, costly imported fuel and scarce industrial land.
  3. Investment climate: red tape, corruption and weak contract enforcement; private investment is stuck near 23% of GDP and FDI below 1% of GDP.
  4. Finance: high non-performing loans and, since 2022, a dollar shortage that hampers imports of machinery and inputs.
  5. Skills and technology: low productivity, weak technical education and the risk of automation.
  6. LDC graduation (scheduled for November 2026): duty-free access and policy space (for example the pharmaceutical patent waiver) will shrink.
  7. Safety and environment: the 2013 Rana Plaza collapse (over 1,100 deaths) and river pollution from dyeing and tanneries.

Conclusion: the prospects are strong, but they will be realised only by diversifying beyond RMG and fixing energy, governance and skills.
pts: Defines industrialisation and states Bangladesh's base (industry over a third of GDP, RMG dominant)
Prospect: large, young, low-cost labour force (demographic dividend)
Prospect: established RMG export base with linkages, or green factories
Prospect: emerging sectors such as pharmaceuticals, leather, light engineering or ICT
Prospect: new infrastructure and economic zones, or a large domestic or regional market
Challenge: narrow export base dependent on RMG
Challenge: energy, gas, power or land constraints
Challenge: poor investment climate, governance, low private investment or FDI, or financial-sector weakness
Challenge: low skills and productivity, or LDC graduation losing trade preferences
Challenge: workplace safety or pollution, with a concluding judgement on diversification

5a.watch:
• The question has two verbs: "explain the prospects" and "what are the challenges". Give each a reason, not a bare list.
  • No course slides cover this topic; the shares (RMG about 84% of exports, private investment about 23% of GDP, FDI below 1%) are public estimates that change yearly, so write "about". The labour force figure is hum-dim slide 7.
  • LDC graduation is scheduled for 24 November 2026 (printed in Q6a of the same paper), though the course SDG slides note a deferral being sought; the EU keeps duty-free access for a three-year transition after graduation.

5b.html:
• Balanced growth (Nurkse, Rosenstein-Rodan) is simultaneous investment in many complementary industries, and in agriculture and industry together, so that each creates the market for the others. It attacks the small size of the market: one factory alone cannot sell its output to a poor population.
  • Unbalanced growth (Hirschman, 1958) is deliberate investment in a few key sectors with the strongest backward and forward linkages. The shortages and surpluses this creates send profit signals that induce investment elsewhere: development as a "chain of disequilibria", which economises on scarce decision-making ability.
  • Big push (Rosenstein-Rodan, 1943; formalised by Murphy, Shleifer and Vishny) is a minimum critical mass of coordinated investment, usually public-led, needed to escape a low-level trap. Because of indivisibilities and demand spillovers (coordination failure), each firm is profitable only if many invest together, so two equilibria exist.
AspectBalanced growthUnbalanced growthBig push
Main obstaclesmall marketscarce capital and decision-makingcoordination failure, indivisibilities
Patternall sectors togetherleading sectors first, others followone large jump to a better equilibrium
Resources neededvery largesmaller, concentratedvery large at the start
Main criticismunaffordable for a poor countrybottlenecks, inflation, regional gapsneeds state capacity; debt risk

The big push is the general case; balanced growth is one way to deliver it, and unbalanced growth is the rival sequential strategy.

Bangladesh context

  • Unbalanced: growth was led by RMG since the 1980s. Its backward linkages (spinning, knitting, dyeing, accessories, packaging) and forward linkages (ports, banking, logistics) pulled in other investment.
  • Big push: the 2010s wave of megaprojects (Padma Bridge, Metro Rail, Rooppur, Karnaphuli tunnel, Matarbari port) and the planned 100 economic zones is a coordinated push, along Hirschman's "excess SOC" path.
  • Balanced elements: five-year plans balance agriculture (rice self-sufficiency) with industry, but resources are too scarce for growth balanced across all sectors.

Conclusion: Bangladesh's record fits RMG-led unbalanced growth plus an infrastructure push; it now needs more balanced diversification, because one-product dependence and project debt are the risks.
pts: Balanced growth: simultaneous investment in complementary sectors that create markets for each other (Nurkse's market-size argument)
Unbalanced growth: investment in key sectors with strongest linkages; imbalances induce further investment (Hirschman)
Big push: a minimum critical mass of coordinated investment because of indivisibilities or coordination failure (Rosenstein-Rodan)
Difference in the obstacle each addresses: market size, scarce decision-making or resources, coordination failure
Difference in pattern: simultaneous, sequential chain of disequilibria, or one large jump between equilibria
Difference in resources needed or in the role of the state
States how the three relate (for example balanced growth as one form of the big push and unbalanced growth as the sequential rival; any sound link earns this)
A criticism of each strategy (cost, bottlenecks or inflation, capacity or debt)
Bangladesh as unbalanced growth: RMG as leading sector with backward and forward linkages
Bangladesh as big push: megaprojects or economic zones as a coordinated investment drive
Bangladesh's balanced elements (agriculture and industry in the plans) and why full balance is unaffordable
A reasoned judgement for Bangladesh (any sound view, for example that megaproject debt makes the push risky, earns this)

5b.watch:
• The question asks for differences: three separate descriptions with no comparison lose about a third of the marks. A comparison table is the fastest way.
  • No course slides cover these theories. The big push follows Todaro chapter 4; balanced and unbalanced growth (Nurkse 1953, Hirschman 1958) follow standard development texts.
  • Hirschman's sharpest criticism of balanced growth: a country able to invest in every sector at once would not be underdeveloped in the first place.
  • The diagrams are optional here (the question does not ask for one) but help to show the paths.

6b.html:
Planning is the deliberate effort of a government to choose social objectives, set quantitative targets to be reached in a given period, and organise the resources and policies to reach them. An economic plan is the document that sets out those targets and the strategy. Plans may be comprehensive (the whole economy) or partial (one sector), and long-term (perspective), medium-term (five-year) or annual. The case for planning in developing countries is market failure, the need to mobilise and allocate scarce resources, coordination of investment, and the requirement of donors.

Steps of planning

  1. Survey of resources and the present situation: data on output, saving, labour, foreign exchange and the main problems.
  2. Objectives and priorities: for example growth, employment, poverty reduction, regional balance; ranked, because they compete.
  3. Targets: quantitative and mutually consistent. The growth target fixes the investment needed through the Harrod-Domar relation I/Y = c\,g (capital-output ratio c, growth g).
  4. Plan formulation in three stages: aggregate (macro growth model for saving, investment and imports), sectoral (input-output allocation among agriculture, industry, power, etc.) and project (selection by social cost-benefit analysis: NPV, IRR, shadow prices).
  5. Financing and approval: domestic saving, taxes and foreign aid; approval by the highest economic body.
  6. Implementation: through annual development programmes, the budget and policies (taxes, credit, prices).
  7. Monitoring, evaluation and revision: progress is checked, the plan is revised, and lessons feed the next plan.

Real-life example: Bangladesh's Eighth Five Year Plan (July 2020 to June 2025)

  • Prepared by the General Economics Division of the Planning Commission after surveying the economy hit by COVID-19 (steps 1 to 2).
  • Objectives: rapid recovery, inclusive growth, jobs, poverty reduction, LDC graduation and the SDGs, within the Perspective Plan 2021-2041.
  • Targets: GDP growth of about 8.5% by FY2025 and poverty down to about 15.6%; the investment needed, about 37% of GDP, implies c \approx 37/8.5 \approx 4.4 (step 3).
  • Sector strategies and projects, approved by the National Economic Council in December 2020 (steps 4 to 5).
  • Implemented through yearly Annual Development Programmes; monitored by the Implementation Monitoring and Evaluation Division (IMED); growth targets in later budgets were cut after the 2022 shocks (steps 6 to 7).

Conclusion: planning is a continuous cycle; its success depends less on the document than on data, implementation and revision.
pts: Defines planning: government chooses objectives, sets quantitative targets for a period and organises resources and policies to reach them
Types of plan or the rationale for planning (market failure, resource mobilisation, coordination, donor requirement)
Step: survey of resources and the present situation
Step: objectives and priorities
Step: consistent quantitative targets, for example investment from I/Y = cg
Step: formulation in aggregate, sectoral and project stages, with cost-benefit appraisal of projects
Step: financing (saving, taxes, aid) and approval
Step: implementation through annual programmes, budget and policies
Step: monitoring, evaluation and revision, feeding the next plan
Real-life example with its objectives and targets (the Eighth Five Year Plan, or any real plan with its specifics)
Example followed through the later steps: approval, implementation and monitoring or revision
Concludes that planning is a continuous cycle that depends on implementation
6b.src: Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 600-604, 610-613; Standard textbook treatment
6b.watch:
• Any real plan earns the example marks if it is followed through the steps: a five-year plan, the Padma Bridge project, or a firm's plan. A bare name with no steps earns little.
  • Targets from memory: the Eighth Plan aimed at about 8.5% growth by FY2025 and about 15.6% poverty, with investment of about 37% of GDP. Quote them with "about"; the example marks do not depend on the exact numbers, and the ratio c \approx 4.4 is an illustration, not a required step.
  • Textbooks list the steps differently (five to eight); credit any sensible sequence that runs from survey to monitoring. Todaro's "three stages" (aggregate, sectoral, project) are stages of plan formulation, not the whole process.
  • The course has no slides on planning; this follows Todaro section 11.2-11.3 and standard texts.

7a.html:
Yes, in part. Both are infrastructure, a means rather than an end: they help several SDGs but cannot deliver them alone.

The projects. The Padma Multipurpose Bridge (6.15 km, road from June 2022, rail from 2023) links about 21 south-western districts and Mongla and Payra ports to Dhaka. The Metro Rail (MRT Line 6, Uttara to Motijheel, about 20 km, from December 2022) is Dhaka's first electric mass transit.

Goals and how

  • SDG 9 (resilient infrastructure, industrialisation): both are core infrastructure; Padma opens the south-west to factories, economic zones and port traffic.
  • SDG 8 (growth, jobs): cheaper, faster transport raises trade and investment; appraisals expected Padma alone to add about 1.2% to GDP.
  • SDGs 1, 2 and 10 (poverty, hunger, inequality): south-west farmers and fishers reach Dhaka markets the same day, get better prices and new jobs, narrowing the regional gap.
  • SDG 11 (cities): Metro gives safe, affordable, accessible public transport (target 11.2) and eases congestion.
  • SDGs 13 and 3 (climate, health): electric trains cut emissions and air pollution; both cut accidents and speed access to hospitals.
  • SDG 5 (gender): safe metro travel (women's coaches) widens women's access to jobs and study.
  • SDG 17: Padma was self-financed (about Tk 30,000 crore); the Metro is a partnership with Japan (JICA).

Limits. Cost overruns and loans strain the budget; one metro line limits reach; tolls and fares may exclude the poor; land acquisition displaces people. Gains need economic zones, power, skills and maintenance.

Conclusion: they advance SDGs 8, 9 and 11 directly and 1, 2, 3, 5, 10 and 13 indirectly, but goals such as 4, 6 and 16 need other policies.
pts: Clear position: they help, but as enablers rather than a full route to the SDGs
Describes the two projects (Padma links the south-west to Dhaka and ports; Metro is electric mass transit in Dhaka)
SDG 9: resilient infrastructure and industrialisation, explained
SDG 8: growth, trade, investment and jobs, or time saved
SDGs 1, 2 and 10: market access for south-western farmers, poverty and regional inequality
SDG 11: safe, affordable urban transport and less congestion
SDG 13 or 3: lower emissions and air pollution, fewer accidents, access to health care (SDG 5 or 17 links also earn this)
Limits: cost and debt, coverage, affordability, resettlement or environmental costs, need for complementary policies
Conclusion naming the goals helped directly and those needing other measures
7a.src: Bangladesh and the SDGs (2026), slides 6-7, 11, 13, 15; Ch 1 Economic development (Todaro), slides 27-33; Standard textbook treatment
7a.watch:
• The question says "if so, which goals and how": name each goal by number and give the mechanism, not a list of numbers.
  • The slides do not cover these projects; the facts above (length, dates, cost, the GDP estimate) are widely reported but approximate. The GDP figure is a pre-construction appraisal estimate, not a measured result.
  • A student who argues "no" can still earn the marks by showing which goals the projects touch and why that is not enough.

7b.html:
Dependence is the reliance of developing countries on developed countries' markets, capital and policies to stimulate their own growth; it extends to adopting rich-country education, technology, institutions and consumption patterns. Its counterpart, dominance, is the far greater power of rich countries over trade, prices and finance. Dependence theory calls the rich countries the centre and the poor the periphery.

How developing countries depend on rich ones

  1. Trade and markets: exports go mostly to rich markets and earn the foreign exchange for imports. Bangladesh's garments, 84% of its exports, sell mainly to the EU and USA; primary-commodity exporters face falling terms of trade (Prebisch-Singer).
  2. Finance: aid, concessional loans, foreign direct investment and remittances fill saving and foreign-exchange gaps, and leave external debt.
  3. Technology and skills: machinery, patents and higher training come from the North, often labour-saving and ill-suited to labour-rich economies.
  4. Policy and institutions: IMF and World Bank conditions, trade rules and preferences (EU duty-free access for least developed countries), and imported "expert" models (the false-paradigm model).
  5. Culture and elites: copied education systems and consumption patterns; local elites (comprador groups) tied to foreign interests.

How the opposite holds: rich countries depend on developing ones

  1. Raw materials and energy: oil and gas, metals, and battery minerals such as cobalt, lithium and rare earths.
  2. Cheap manufactures and supply chains: rich-country consumers and firms rely on low-cost garments, electronics and parts from Asia.
  3. Markets and profits: fast-growing middle classes buy rich-country goods, services and capital equipment; multinationals repatriate profits and lenders earn interest.
  4. Labour: migrant workers in care, construction and farming, and skilled migrants such as doctors and engineers.
  5. Global public goods: climate stability (tropical forests, future emissions), pandemic control and security need developing-country cooperation.

Conclusion: the relationship is interdependence, but unequal. Developing countries rely on markets and capital they cannot influence, while rich countries can usually switch suppliers. Dependence theorists see this as a cause of underdevelopment; South Korea, which grew through export ties with rich countries, shows the ties can also be used for development.
pts: Defines dependence (reliance on rich-country markets, capital, policies and models), with dominance or centre and periphery
Trade and market dependence, with an example (garments sold to the EU and USA, or falling terms of trade)
Financial dependence: aid, loans, foreign investment or remittances, and the debt that follows
Dependence on rich-country technology and skills, possibly inappropriate to labour-rich economies
Policy and institutional dependence: IMF or World Bank conditions, trade rules or preferences, false-paradigm advice
Cultural or elite dependence (education, consumption patterns, comprador groups), or another sound kind
Opposite: rich countries need developing-country raw materials and energy
Opposite: rich countries rely on cheap manufactures and global supply chains
Opposite: developing countries are markets for rich-country goods and capital and a source of profits and interest
Opposite: migrant and skilled labour from developing countries
Opposite: global public goods (climate, health, security) or another sound example such as holdings of rich-country debt
Concludes that the relationship is interdependence but unequal, with a view on dependence theory
7b.src: Ch 3 Classic theories, slides 30, 34; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 170-174, 182; Bangladesh and the SDGs (2026), slide 6
7b.watch:
• The second part asks how rich countries depend on poor ones; an answer that lists only aid and trade from the developing side earns half the marks.
  • Keep the "kinds" distinct (trade, finance, technology, policy, culture); repeating "aid" under several headings earns one point.
  • The 84% share is from the course's SDG deck; the destination markets (mainly the EU and USA) are widely reported, not from the slides.

8a.html:
Measuring inequality. Relative inequality is measured from the size distribution of income: households are ranked from poorest to richest and grouped into quintiles (fifths), and each group's share of total income is found.

  • Lorenz curve: cumulative % of income plotted against cumulative % of population. The diagonal is the line of perfect equality; the more the curve bows below it, the more unequal the distribution.
  • Gini coefficient: the area A between the diagonal and the curve over the whole triangle A + B under the diagonal, from 0 (equality) to 1 (perfect inequality). From quintile data the area under the curve is a sum of trapezoids:
G = \frac{A}{A+B} = 1 - \sum_{k=1}^{5} (X_k - X_{k-1})(Y_k + Y_{k-1})

where X and Y are the cumulative population and income shares as fractions.

Bangladesh and the US. Quintile shares (Table 5.2, Bangladesh 2005, US 2000), cumulated:

Cumulative population20%40%60%80%100%
Bangladesh, cumulative income %9.422.038.159.2100
United States, cumulative income %5.416.131.854.2100
\begin{aligned} G_{BD} &= 1 - 0.2\,(0.094 + 0.314 + 0.601 + 0.973 + 1.592) = 1 - 0.715 = 0.29 \\ G_{US} &= 1 - 0.2\,(0.054 + 0.215 + 0.479 + 0.860 + 1.542) = 1 - 0.630 = 0.37 \end{aligned}

Comparison.

  • Bangladesh's Lorenz curve lies above the US curve at every point, closer to the diagonal. By the Lorenz criterion Bangladesh is unambiguously more equal: its poorest 40% get 22.0% of income against 16.1%, its richest 20% get 40.8% against 45.8%.
  • The Gini agrees: 0.29 against 0.37 from these quintiles (survey estimates 0.32 for Bangladesh in 2010 and 0.415 for the US in 2016).
  • This is relative inequality only: the US has far higher income per head.
pts: Size distribution: rank by income, group into quintiles or deciles, find each group's income share
Lorenz curve: cumulative % of income against cumulative % of population; diagonal = perfect equality; more bow = more inequality
Gini = A/(A+B), from 0 (equality) to 1 (perfect inequality)
Shows how the Gini is computed from grouped data (trapezoids), or reads it as twice the area between the diagonal and the curve
Cumulative shares for both countries (Table 5.2 values, or a schematic with the Bangladesh curve clearly nearer the diagonal)
Sketch: both curves on one labelled diagram with the diagonal, Bangladesh above the US
Compares: Bangladesh's curve lies above the US curve everywhere, so it is unambiguously more equal (for example 22.0% against 16.1% for the poorest 40%)
Gini comparison: Bangladesh's Gini is lower (about 0.29 against 0.37 from Table 5.2, or 0.32 against 0.415; a schematic answer that states the order earns it)
Notes that this is relative inequality, not the level of income
8a.sketch:
• Square box with both axes 0 to 100%: cumulative % of population (x) and of income (y).
  • Diagonal labelled "line of perfect equality".
  • Bangladesh curve above the US curve at every point, both meeting the diagonal at 0 and 100%.
  • Area A between the diagonal and a curve marked, with G = A/(A + B).
8a.src: Ch 5 Poverty and inequality, slides 6-15, 34-35, 47; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 263-269, 281-285
8a.watch:
• The paper gives no data, so a neat schematic with Bangladesh's curve nearer the diagonal earns the drawing marks; numbers from the slides' Table 5.2 make the comparison stronger.
  • The quintile Ginis (0.29, 0.37) sit below the survey values (0.32, 0.415) for two reasons: five points hide inequality inside each fifth (a grouped Gini is a lower bound), and the survey values are for later years (2010, 2016).
  • Bangladesh's shares are most likely consumption (expenditure) shares and the US ones income shares; consumption is more evenly spread, so the gap is probably somewhat overstated.
  • Do not say Bangladesh is "better off": a more equal Lorenz curve says nothing about poverty or average income.

8b.html:
Tied aid is bilateral aid (a grant or loan) that the recipient must spend on goods and services from the donor country (tied by source), or only on a project the donor specifies (tied by project). Untied aid can be spent anywhere. A concessional loan carries interest and must be repaid, but on softer terms than the market.

Drawbacks of tied aid

  1. Higher prices. The recipient cannot shop around, and donor firms are often costly or monopolistic; studies put the extra cost at roughly 15 to 30%, so the real value of aid is well below its face value.
  2. Inappropriate technology. Capital-intensive equipment suits the donor, not a labour-abundant economy: few jobs, and lock-in to the donor's spare parts and experts.
  3. Donor-chosen projects displace national priorities; new machinery may be bought while existing capacity stands idle.
  4. Aid returns to the donor. Much of the money is spent on the donor's consultants, contractors and shipping, so tied aid acts as an export subsidy for the donor.
  5. Delays and political leverage. Donor procurement rules add delays and costs, and conditions reduce the recipient's policy freedom.

Why interest-bearing loans make it worse

  1. Inflated cost repaid with interest. The overpricing is borrowed, so the recipient repays it with interest; the grant element of the loan shrinks further.
  2. Repayment in foreign exchange. Debt service uses export earnings, so a loan meant to close the foreign-exchange gap later widens it, especially when the project (a road) earns only local currency.
  3. Exchange-rate risk. When the taka fell from about Tk 86 to about Tk 120 per US dollar (2022 to 2024), the taka cost of every dollar repaid rose by about 40%.
  4. Debt burden. Bangladesh's external debt service rose by about a quarter to about USD 3.36 billion in FY2023-24 as megaproject grace periods ended. Sri Lanka's 2022 default shows what happens when debt service outruns foreign-exchange earnings.

Bangladesh examples: Indian lines of credit require about 75% of goods and services from India (about 65% for civil works); Japan's STEP loans and Russia's credit for Rooppur use donor-country prime contractors.

Conclusion: tied, interest-bearing aid gives less development per dollar and leaves debt; recipients should negotiate untied, highly concessional terms and borrow only for projects whose returns cover the full cost.
pts: Defines tied aid: must be spent on donor-country goods and services or on donor-specified projects (contrasted with untied aid)
Higher prices because the recipient cannot shop around, so the real value is below face value (the 15 to 30% estimate is optional)
Inappropriate capital-intensive technology, few jobs, dependence on donor parts and experts
Donor-chosen projects distort priorities, or machinery is bought while capacity stands idle
Much of the aid returns to donor consultants and firms: an export subsidy for the donor
Delays, procurement costs or political conditions
Loans: the inflated cost is repaid with interest, so the grant element shrinks
Loans: debt service in foreign exchange drains export earnings and widens the foreign-exchange gap
Loans: exchange-rate risk raises the local-currency cost of repayment
Loans: growing debt burden (an example such as Bangladesh's rising debt service is optional) and a conclusion on better terms
8b.src: Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 806-807, 810-815; Standard textbook treatment
8b.watch:
• The question stresses "especially interest-bearing loans": at least a third of the answer should show how tying and interest compound, not only list the costs of tying.
  • The 15 to 30% overpricing is a commonly cited range from OECD-era studies, not a precise figure; say "roughly".
  • The debt-service figure (about USD 3.36 billion in FY2023-24), the 75% Indian-content rule and the taka rate (about 86 to about 120 per dollar, 2022 to 2024) are press-reported ERD and Bangladesh Bank data quoted from memory: write "about"; no marks depend on them. No course slides cover this topic; the argument follows Todaro chapter 14.
  • Sri Lanka's default came mostly from market borrowing (sovereign bonds), not only from project loans; use it as a warning about debt service, not as a debt-trap story.
  • Do not confuse tied aid with conditionality: conditions attach policies to aid; tying restricts where the money is spent.
